title: Wheeler Creek
subtitle: Wheeler Canyon, Utah — A Late-Night Detour
summary:
## The Pivoted Plan

We were geared up, hyped up, and ready to conquer Sardine Loop at Snow Basin. Nature, however, had other plans. When we arrived, we found the access road firmly closed, forcing a quick rethink of our entire weekend. It was already 8:00 PM—a notoriously terrible time to start hunting for a campsite—and we needed a backup fast.

Enter Dad's memory banks. Strolling back through 5 to 7 years of hiking and mountain biking trails, he recalled a spot next to Wheeler Creek in Wheeler Canyon. It was a complete gamble for a crew campout, but with the sun rapidly sinking, we took the detour and headed in.

## Camp Setup in the Deep Dark

By the time we completed the one-mile hike and reached the creek, night had fully claimed the canyon. It wasn't just dark; it was a dense, wrap-around forest darkness. Out came the headlamps and flashlights, turning our camp setup into a chaotic light show of shadows and tent poles. Lina (Dad's daughter) set up with Dad in one tent, while Keishin and Perrin claimed the second.

Leaving so late meant dinner had been sorted for everyone—except Keishin, whose stomach was staging a protest. Thankfully, we had made a tactical pitstop at Smith's on the way up to buy him a pack of instant Ramen. Firing up the camp stove in the pitch black felt like a high-stakes culinary performance, but the water boiled, the noodles cooked, and Keishin was saved from starvation.

## Late-Night Comedy & The Sleeping Pad Reviews

The bottom of the canyon was a velvet pocket: no moon, heavy tree cover, and the loud, rushing hum of the creek providing the ultimate ambient white noise.

Once the tents were zipped, the crew split into two different worlds. In the boys' tent, Perrin and Keishin stayed up late laughing and joking like they were hosting a late-night talk show. In the other tent, Lina fell asleep almost instantly, while Dad lay awake reading his Kindle, probably staying up later than everyone else in the end.

It was a comfortable 61°F night, leading to some very passionate gear reviews. Keishin test-drove our new Nemo sleeping pad and declared it an absolute luxury. Lina slept like a log on the old Klymit inflatable pad. Dad, however, was having a minor crisis on his premium Exped pad—his Nemo down sleeping bag was so incredibly warm he had to spend half the night trying to find a way to cool off.

## Rise of the Butterflies of the Night

Morning in the canyon was pure bliss. Thanks to the towering canyon walls and the thick forest canopy acting as natural blackout curtains, the sun was blocked from baking our tents. For once on a camping trip, we got to sleep in.

As the morning rolled on, we could hear the faint crunch of early-bird hikers and the whir of mountain bikes on the main trail nearby. But screened behind our green wall of trees, we were completely invisible and secluded.

Lina spotted a few fluttering visitors and officially dubbed the local moths the "butterflies of the night." We also shared the camp with some giant, prehistoric-looking ants, though they politely minded their own business.

## The Stowaway Squeak

After packing up and hiking the mile back to the car (stopping to snap our morning trail photo along the way), we loaded up, proud of a successful pivot. Then came the grand finale.

Sitting in the car ready to drive home, Dad looked down at his hand and froze. Staring back at him from just below his thumb was a massive, inch-long bug. Naturally, Dad reacted with the dignified grace of a seasoned outdoorsman: he squeaked, panicked, and thrashed his hand. The bug went airborne, flying straight over to Lina's side of the car.

Lina didn't even notice, but we all piled out of the car for an emergency search-and-rescue mission. We searched every crevice but found nothing. Reluctantly, we got back in and started the drive.

Partway home, Keishin spotted the hitchhiker. We executed a swift roadside pull-over, and Dad harmlessly flicked the intruder out of the window. We still have no idea what kind of bug it was, but it gave us one last laugh on a fantastic, spontaneous detour.
